newsitem.title: UK: Sentiment improving on North Europe grains markets.
newsitem.headline: Sentiment improving on North Europe grains markets.

text.p: Northern European grain markets ended the week buoyed by sentiment that the supply balance is tighter than earlier thought.
Export optimism led, helped by an EU tender which was seen as a concession to traders desperate to fill order books.
Markets further south were more subdued.
French port prices for wheat climbed again this week, pulling up most of the domestic grain complex as European buyers scratched around for cover, traders said.

Wheat at Rouen rose nearly one percent as sellers sensed rising panic in a group of exporters left without European Union licences, although licence-switching and a higher EU export award allayed some concerns in the short term.
Market action at the ports drove prices higher inland where wheat for delivery to northern Europe was marked up 10 francs to 810 francs a tonne, basis fob Creil, dealers said.
Flooding on the Moselle river added to a similar picture in eastern France where wheat for delivery to Germany gained up to 7.50 francs at 840 francs, dealers said.
The Moselle burst its banks this week but so far traffic has been switching successfully to the Rhine.

Other bullish signs included inquiries from animal feed manufacturers worried about prices and the prospect of further upward pressure on underlying grain after flour exporters booked around 600,000 tonnes of European Union licences.
But traders said most players were treading carefully amid signs the European Commission still wants internal prices down. Many were anxious to smooth out further domestic price rises.
The EU sharply boosted wheat licence awards to 400,000 tonnes on Thursday but turned down bids for another 600,000, including some 120,000 just outside its refund cut-off.
Officials said the reason for this was the market's domestic strength mainly in France.
Maize firmed, dragged up purely by wheat as the virtual completion of maize import allocations to Spain from the United States removed support from the southern continent.
March deliveries at Bordeaux added 7.5 francs a tonne to 852.50 francs but the underlying tone was fragile, dealers said.

German wheat export markets may be on the way to recovery after three months' lull as prices have become more competitive, brokers said. Exporters' readiness to reduce bids for EU export subsidies may get more grain flowing, they added.
Domestic prices and export quotes have fallen steadily in 1997 and monthly storage fees, which are usually added, were not achieved by sellers in Jan/Feb.

Domestic mill buyers and export traders are seeking grain at around 265-270 marks a tonne while German export brokers are looking for 277.50-300 marks fob for spot wheat in a 12-14 percent protein range, down 1.00-2.50 marks from last week.
Brokers say the market may have found its floor, with March storage fees added by sellers and they are also citing export hopes to Poland, Uzbekistan, Bulgaria and the Czech republic.
Increased optimism on exports kept the UK market firm and severed the chains which kept the grains market in a close, inverse, relationship to the sterling/mark rate.
Talk that a 50,000 tonne cargo of wheat was being loaded for China sent prices up on Wednesday and has continued to contribute to the market's strength, traders said.
"The market got badly spooked by the China report," one said. "They still haven't got to the bottom of it."
One exporter confirmed that there was a vessel due to load in Tilbury, but said he could not confirm that it was going to China.
"There's a lot of rumour flying around," he said. "One has to be a little bit sceptical."

The underlying reason for the market's strength was the appearance of more demand news since the start of the year, one trader said. And the EU's big tender award on Thursday helped fuel the argument.
But UK wheat remained uncompetitive against French and Danish supplies, he said.
Spanish dealers said active trade was only seen in the maize market where ex-farm prices rose slightly in the week ending February 28.

In the south, prices rose to as high as 24,000 pesetas per tonne, while in the northern region of Cataluna, prices were around 23,500, and in the central region of Castilla Leon prices were around 22,500.

Spanish wheat prices failed to adopt the strength seen in French and British prices. Dealers said clients were opting for alternative forms of feed including maize and durum wheat trade was almost entirely stagnant.
Barley prices remained largely unchanged although in the Burgos region, prices roses slightly to around 21,200.

Italian cereal markets were again calm this week with no substantial changes. Maize prices fell over the past week due to an increase in supply with no fresh demand, the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies (Ismea) said. Ismea noted rumours on the market of a lack of domestic durum wheat.
